summary: Walter Pater's first letter to Wilde, July 1877 — the only direct contact recorded here, kept because of what it was worth to Wilde.
certainty_reasoning: The record documents a friendship or acquaintance with no evidence of attraction or romance; classified platonic, upgradable if contrary evidence comes to light.

sources.quote: Dear Mr Wilde, Accept my best thanks for the magazine and your letter. Your excellent article on the Grosvenor Gallery I read with very great pleasure: it makes me much wish to make your acquaintance, and I hope you will give me an early call on your return to Oxford. I should much like to talk over some of the points with you, though on the whole I think your criticisms very just, and they are certainly very pleasantly expressed. The article shows that you possess some beautiful, and, for your age, quite exceptionally cultivated tastes: and a considerable knowledge too of many beautiful things. I hope you will write a great deal in time to come. Very truly yours
sources.context: Walter Pater to Oscar Wilde, headed 'Bradmore Road. Oxford. July 14' [1877] (MS Texas), quoted whole. It survives inside a letter of Wilde's to William Ward, who had been sent the original and told to return it by registered post; Wilde then thought better of trusting it to the postman and copied it out instead. Wilde's transcription has three small errors, which the editors list. His own comment follows it: 'You won't think me snobbish for sending you this? After all, it is something to be honestly proud of.' Wilde was twenty-two; the article was his first.
sources.speaker: Walter Pater
sources.supports: The first contact, in Pater's own hand, and what it was worth to Wilde.
